{"id": "19:12/q33", "question": "How did Jesus and Yahya compare one another?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:12/q33/p1", "position": "Each asked the other to seek forgiveness and called the other better.", "reasons": "Hasan's report in Ibn Kathir says Jesus cited God's peace upon Yahya as evidence of merit."}]}
{"id": "19:13/q01", "question": "What does ḥanānan min ladunnā mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the gift is divine tenderness to Yahya, mercy to his parents, tenderness placed in Yahya, love, honor, blessing, or a distinct bond; the phrase 'from Us' and Arabic usage guide the readings.", "positions": [{"id": "19:13/q01/p1", "position": "God's mercy or tender compassion toward Yahya, bestowed from His presence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and many later commentators give mercy; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ say only God can give it. Mujāhid specifically has the Lord's tenderness toward Yahya. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī and others cite Arabic poetry for mercy. Al-Zajjāj includes affection; Ibn Kathīr compares a camel's tenderness for its young. Al-Qurṭubī prefers tenderness while leaving its direction open. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the divine gift exceeds ordinary human measure; al-Asad calls it special. Al-Bāqir's report has God answer Yahya's invocation, 'Here I am, John.'"}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p2", "position": "The gift is mercy to Zakariyyā or both parents through the grant of Yahya.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ reads an accusative of cause and makes the child and answered prayer mercy for the parents; al-Wāḥidī says this requires an ellipsis. Qatāda's report names Zakariyyā. Al-Rāzī adds that the response purifies him from being a rejected supplicant. Ibn al-Anbārī says God acted mercifully toward Yahya's parents."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p3", "position": "God placed mercy, tenderness, or a gentle heart in Yahya for his parents, contemporaries, and other people.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās's Ibn ʿAbbās report says it helped Yahya save people from unbelief and evil. Al-Māwardī adds softening hearts for a prompt response; Abū ʿAlī and al-Wāḥidī connect it to preaching obedience. Al-Rāzī says purity protects mercy from excusing wrongdoing; he and al-Bursawī cite 24:2. Al-Kāshshāf includes parents and others."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p4", "position": "Ḥanān is love or loving affection.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, Ibn Zayd, ʿAwf and Saʿīd al-Juhanī use love; al-Qurṭubī cites spouses' affection in poetry. Al-Wāḥidī records Ibn ʿAbbās tentatively calling it God's affection for His servant. Al-Ālūsī specifies Yahya was made beloved by people, comparing 20:39; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also reports popular love as one reading."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p5", "position": "It means exaltation, honor, or reverence from God.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ b. Abī Rabāḥ gives exaltation. Al-Rāzī cites Waraqa's threat to honor Bilāl if killed as comparable wording. Al-Biqāʿī includes reverence in the divine endowment; Ibn al-Aʿrābī also records a sacred or exalted use."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p6", "position": "It means blessing or provision.", "reasons": "Ibn Jubayr is reported with blessing; Ibn al-Aʿrābī records provision and blessing among the senses, while al-Biqāʿī includes them in the direct gift."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p7", "position": "It is a special divine attraction and bond between Yahya and his Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this because 'from Us' places the gift beyond ordinary causes; he sets aside readings as popular affection or Yahya's compassion for people. Al-Wāsiṭī says the divine tenderness brought Yahya intimacy and expansiveness."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p8", "position": "It describes Yahya's living, vibrant heart and soul.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Yahya's Gospel statements still move people and objects to reports that Ibn ʿAbbās could not understand this common Arabic word."}, {"id": "19:13/q01/p9", "position": "Its meaning was unknown to Ibn ʿAbbās in some reports.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Suyūṭī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ transmit his non-answer, sometimes through Saʿīd b. Jubayr; al-Suyūṭī also lists it among four words Ibn ʿAbbās said he did not know. Iṣlāḥī contests this attribution."}]}
{"id": "19:13/q02", "question": "What do the root and Arabic forms of ḥanān convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the relevant Arabic form is a verbal noun, conventional expression, dialectal form, or dual.", "positions": [{"id": "19:13/q02/p1", "position": "The root moves from longing or yearning to tenderness, compassion, and mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls ḥanān a verbal noun and cites taḥannan and ḥannah in poetry. Al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn Qutayba as transmitted by Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī compare a she-camel's longing for its young; al-Rāzī also recalls the Prophet's moaning palm trunk. Al-Majāz cites Imruʾ al-Qays and al-Ḥuṭayʾa; al-Zajjāj gives two poetry witnesses; al-Ḥuṭayʾa's request to ʿUmar is cited by al-Jishumī."}, {"id": "19:13/q02/p2", "position": "Ḥanānik may be a conventional expression or dialectal form, or a dual expressing repeated compassion.", "reasons": "Al-Majāz, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ record disagreement on dual versus independent or dialectal form. Ṭarafa's line and Imruʾ al-Qays's ḥanānaka are cited. Abū ʿUbayda says the dual is common; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes it as compassion upon compassion."}, {"id": "19:13/q02/p3", "position": "Ḥanān is rare in the Qur'an despite the abundance of mercy vocabulary.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says this form and root occur only here, while forms of r-ḥ-m are frequent; she mentions 18:81."}]}
{"id": "19:13/q03", "question": "How is ḥanānan construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "What omitted or preceding term governs ḥanānan and its case.", "positions": [{"id": "19:13/q03/p1", "position": "It is an accusative coordinated with the earlier gift of judgment; 'We gave' governs it.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī also allows its association with the gift of the Book; Ibn Kathīr says wisdom, affection, and purity are jointly given. Al-Bursawī says indefiniteness magnifies the gift; al-Ālūsī says it amplifies the endowment."}, {"id": "19:13/q03/p2", "position": "It is a causal accusative: God did this as mercy for the parents.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ ties the accusative to the gift of the child. Al-Wāḥidī says the reading needs an ellipsis about the child and answered prayer; al-Ālūsī lists a causal object among the possible parses."}, {"id": "19:13/q03/p3", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun in a supplication with an omitted verb.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ compares suqyan and raʿyan; al-Ālūsī also lists a verbal-noun parse."}, {"id": "19:13/q03/p4", "position": "It may be a nominative predicate with an omitted subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn cites the expression in 12:18; Sibawayh's quoted poem supplies a nominative use of ḥanān."}, {"id": "19:13/q03/p5", "position": "It can attach to the description 'as a child' or be coordinated with ṣabiyyan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ālūsī record this alternative."}]}
{"id": "19:13/q04", "question": "What does min ladunnā add?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase merely names the giver, intensifies the gift, or identifies its special character.", "positions": [{"id": "19:13/q04/p1", "position": "The tenderness is directly and specially bestowed by God.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī glosses it 'from God'; al-Daḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ say none else grants this mercy. Al-Biqāʿī says Yahya received it without teaching or experience; the Study Quran and Asad call it a special divine gift."}, {"id": "19:13/q04/p2", "position": "It qualifies and magnifies the gift of ḥanān.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says it qualifies ḥanān. Al-Ālūsī construes it with an omitted adjective, marking both its innate greatness and its special divine source."}, {"id": "19:13/q04/p3", "position": "It points to a bond beyond ordinary causes between Yahya and God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses the phrase to prefer this reading over people's affection and Yahya's compassion."}]}
{"id": "19:13/q05", "question": "May Ḥannān be used as a name or attribute of God?", "turns_on": "Whether figurative merciful usage suffices or a reliable naming report is required.", "positions": [{"id": "19:13/q05/p1", "position": "It may be applied to God as compassionate and merciful, with figurative language.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Samīn liken the expression to calling Him Raḥīm; al-Rāzī reports permissive usage. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a divine attribute. Ibn al-Aʿrābī distinguishes doubled-n Ḥannān as Merciful from light-n ḥanān as tenderness; Ibn Kathīr transmits a report of a man in Hell invoking 'O Ḥannān, O Mannān' for a thousand years."}, {"id": "19:13/q05/p2", "position": "It should not be established as a divine name.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports an objection from the root's original associations and the absence of a reliable report naming God so."}]}

{"id": "19:15/q01", "question": "What does the salām upon Yahya mean?", "turns_on": "Whether salām is read as protective safety, a greeting that itself honors Yahya, or a commanded greeting.", "positions": [{"id": "19:15/q01/p1", "position": "It is safety and protection for Yahya.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and others gloss it as safety (Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi); al-Kalbi calls it safety from God (Wahidi); Wahidi-Wajiz and Ibn Kathir apply it throughout the named stages.
